items.name: Bias & variance

resource.label: CampusX · 100 Days of ML · Bias-Variance trade-off · 8 min

items.note: Bias is error from wrong assumptions (underfitting). Variance is sensitivity to the particular training sample (overfitting). As a statistics term, an estimator is biased if its average over many samples misses the true value. That's why sample variance divides by n−1.

items.name: Sampling techniques

resource.label: Wikipedia · Sampling methods

items.note: Simple random sampling: everyone has an equal chance. Stratified: sample within each group so small groups are represented (stratify=y in train_test_split). Cluster: pick whole groups. Systematic: every k-th item. Convenience samples are biased.

resource.label: CampusX · Maths for ML · S43 Binomial & CLT @ 57:05–1:06:57 Intuition of Central Limit Theorem (CLT) · 10 min

items.note: It's shown in code at 1:06:57. Sample means are roughly normal whatever the population's shape, once n ≳ 30.

items.name: Law of Large Numbers

resource.label: Wikipedia · Law of large numbers

items.note: As the sample grows, the sample mean converges to the true mean: flip a coin 10 times and you may get 70% heads, flip it 10,000 times and you'll be near 50%. That's why evaluations on 20 examples are noisy. The LLN says the average converges, the CLT (row above) says how the average is distributed.

items.name: Outliers & robustness

resource.label: CampusX · 100 Days of ML · What are Outliers @ 0:51–4:40 What are outliers? · 4 min

items.note: Robust statistics resist outliers. The median and IQR barely move when you add one extreme value, while the mean and standard deviation can swing a lot.

items.name: Entropy

resource.label: CampusX · Entropy in Decision Trees @ 0:29–2:23 What is Entropy? · 2 min

items.note: H = −Σ p log p, which measures uncertainty. A fair coin has 1 bit and a certain outcome has 0.

items.name: Cross-entropy

resource.label: CampusX · 100 Days of DL · Loss Functions @ 11:08–14:20 Cross-entropy — Loss functions in deep learning · 3 min

items.note: The loss list here includes binary and categorical cross-entropy. H(p, q) = −Σ p log q: the true distribution p, scored against the predicted q. With a one-hot label it reduces to −log(probability given to the right class). LLM training loss is exactly this, per token.

items.name: KL divergence

resource.label: Wikipedia · KL divergence

items.note: No CampusX video covers this. KL(p‖q) = Σ p log(p/q) = cross-entropy − entropy. It's the extra cost of using q when the truth is p. It's ≥ 0, and it isn't symmetric. It shows up in RLHF (the KL penalty that keeps the model near the base model), in distillation and in VAEs.

items.name: Information gain

resource.label: CampusX · 100 Days of ML · Decision Trees, Entropy, Info Gain @ 36:20–41:40 Information Gain · 5 min

items.note: Information gain = entropy of the parent − weighted entropy of the children. The "also" link works a full example.

items.name: Why cross-entropy is used in classification

resource.label: CampusX · 100 Days of ML · Logistic Regression 4 Loss & Max Likelihood @ 4:48–29:02 Why cross-entropy — Maximum Likelihood · 24 min

items.note: Why cross-entropy for classification: (1) minimising it is exactly maximum likelihood; (2) it punishes confident wrong answers hard (−log 0.01 = 4.6); (3) with softmax or sigmoid, its gradient is simply (prediction − label), which doesn't vanish, whereas MSE plus sigmoid gives weak gradients when the model is badly wrong.

items.name: Manhattan distance

resource.label: Wikipedia · Taxicab (Manhattan) distance

items.note: Manhattan distance = Σ abs(aᵢ − bᵢ), like walking city blocks. From (1, 2) to (4, 6): Manhattan = 3 + 4 = 7, Euclidean = 5. It's less dominated by one large difference than Euclidean.

items.note: In high dimensions, points become nearly equidistant and most of the volume sits near the edges, so distance-based methods (kNN) weaken and you need exponentially more data.

resource.label: CampusX · Maths for ML · Joint, Marginal, Conditional, Bayes @ 17:49–27:44 Multivariate (joint) — Joint Probability · 10 min

items.note: A multivariate distribution is a joint distribution over several variables at once, P(X, Y). This is joint probability for discrete variables. The continuous version you'll meet most is the multivariate normal (the "also" link).

items.name: Gaussian distribution in higher dimensions

resource.label: CampusX · Maths for ML · S41 Normal Distribution @ 31:03–37:15 Gaussian in 2D — 2D Density plots · 6 min

items.note: The 2D density plot is the picture. N(μ, Σ) has a mean vector μ and a covariance matrix Σ. Its contours are ellipses whose axes are Σ's eigenvectors. Diagonal Σ means independent features.

items.name: Covariance matrix interpretation

resource.label: CampusX · 100 Days of ML · PCA Part 2 Problem formulation @ 12:55–23:17 Covariance and Covariance Matrix · 10 min

items.note: The diagonal holds each feature's variance and off the diagonal are the covariances. It's symmetric, and its eigenvectors are the principal components.

items.name: Mahalanobis distance

resource.label: Wikipedia · Mahalanobis distance

items.note: Mahalanobis distance = √((x−μ)ᵀ Σ⁻¹ (x−μ)): Euclidean distance after undoing the correlations and scales in the data. It's used for anomaly detection. With Σ = I it reduces to Euclidean.

items.name: Eigen decomposition

resource.label: CampusX · 100 Days of ML · PCA Part 2 Problem formulation @ 35:35–38:04 Eigendecompostion of a covariance Matrix · 2 min

items.note: A = QΛQ⁻¹. For a symmetric matrix like a covariance matrix, A = QΛQᵀ with orthogonal Q.

items.name: Singular Value Decomposition (SVD)

resource.label: Wikipedia · Singular value decomposition

items.note: CampusX's SVD session is members-only. A = UΣVᵀ works for any matrix (even non-square): rotate, scale along axes, rotate. Keeping the top k singular values gives the best rank-k approximation. That idea is behind LoRA (low-rank weight updates) and compression. np.linalg.svd(A).

items.note: Why reduce dimensions: fewer features means less overfitting and faster training, and you can visualise the data in 2D. Embedding models do the same thing by compressing text into a few hundred dimensions.

items.note: Hypothesis-driven debugging: state what you expected vs what happened, list 2–3 possible causes, and design a quick check that separates them (a print, an assert, a smaller input). Run it, discard the wrong causes, repeat. Ask the AI for hypotheses and checks, not for a guess at a fix.

items.note: Make the model reason before editing: explore → plan → code → verify. Plan mode (the "also" link, CampusX) forces the plan step so you can review it first.

resource.label: Fixing edge cases

items.note: Edge cases to ask about explicitly: empty input, a single item, duplicates, None/NaN, very large input, unicode, timezones, concurrent calls, network failure. Ask "which edge cases does this code not handle?", then turn each answer into a test.

items.name: Big-O notation

resource.label: CampusX · Python for ML · Algorithm Complexity, Big O · 73 min

items.note: Big-O describes how cost grows with n, ignoring constants. O(1) dict lookup, O(log n) binary search, O(n) scan, O(n log n) sort, O(n²) nested loops. The "also" link is the cost of every Python list, dict and set operation.

items.name: Time vs space complexity

resource.label: CampusX · Algorithms · Space and Time Complexity · 5 min

items.note: Time is how many steps, space is how much extra memory. Caching trades space for time, as in memoisation or a KV cache.

items.name: Best / average / worst case

resource.label: Wikipedia · Best, worst and average case

items.note: Quicksort is O(n log n) on average but O(n²) in the worst case (already sorted input with a bad pivot). A dict lookup is O(1) on average and O(n) in the worst case (many collisions). Big-O usually quotes the worst case unless stated.

items.name: Arrays & strings

resource.label: CampusX · Python for AI · S4 Lists @ 11:34–13:40 Arrays (lists) — what are Lists · 2 min

items.note: A Python list is a dynamic array: O(1) index and append, O(n) insert or delete at the front. Strings are immutable arrays of characters. The "also" link is string problems.

items.name: Linked lists

resource.label: CampusX · Linked Lists in Python · Part 1 · 14 min

items.note: Parts 2–9 of the same playlist implement insertion, traversal and deletion.

items.name: Stacks

resource.label: CampusX · Data Structures · Intro to Stacks @ 0:14–1:00 What is a Stack · 1 min

items.note: In Python a list is a stack: append and pop, both O(1). Used for undo, parsing brackets and DFS.

items.name: Queues & deques

resource.label: CampusX · Data Structures · Intro to Queues @ 0:13–1:19 Q Data Structure · 1 min

items.note: Use collections.deque (the "also" link): O(1) at both ends, whereas list.pop(0) is O(n). Used for BFS and sliding windows.

items.name: Hash maps & sets

resource.label: Python docs · Dictionaries (hash maps)

items.note: dict and set are hash tables: O(1) average lookup, insert and delete. Keys must be hashable (immutable). Swapping a list for a set in "x in items" is the most common real-world speed-up.

items.name: Heaps / priority queues

resource.label: CampusX · Data Structures · Priority Queue @ 0:12–0:54 Priority queue — ABOUT PRIORITY QUEUE · 1 min

items.note: The concept is covered here (in C). In Python use heapq (the "also" link): heappush/heappop in O(log n), and nlargest(k, xs) for top-k, which is how you'd take the top-k similarity scores.

items.name: Trees & binary search trees

resource.label: CampusX · Binary Search Tree Implementation (Python) · 40 min

items.note: In a BST, left < node < right, so search is O(log n) when balanced and O(n) when degenerate. Inorder traversal (32:58) gives the values in sorted order.

items.name: Graphs (representations)

resource.label: CampusX · Data Structures · Intro to Graphs @ 3:07–5:12 REPRESENTATION OF GRAPH · 2 min

items.note: In Python an adjacency list is a dict: graph = {"A": ["B", "C"], ...}. Agent workflows (LangGraph) and knowledge graphs are graphs.

items.name: Sorting (merge, quick)

resource.label: CampusX · Algorithms · Quick Sort · 14 min

items.note: CampusX has quick sort (in C) and no merge sort. Merge sort (the "also" link): split in half, sort each half, merge, always O(n log n), stable, O(n) extra space. Quick sort: partition around a pivot, O(n log n) on average, in place. Python's sorted() is Timsort (merge-based, stable).

items.name: Binary search

resource.label: CampusX · Algorithms · Binary Search @ 1:37–2:26 Steps · 1 min

items.note: Binary search halves a sorted range each step: O(log n). In Python, use bisect (the "also" link). The recursive version is at youtube.com/watch?v=0qBo12QYmOY.

items.name: Two pointers & sliding window

resource.label: CampusX · Problem Solving · Two Pointer Approach · 10 min

items.note: A sliding window keeps a range [left, right] and moves the ends instead of recomputing, e.g. max sum of k consecutive items in O(n) instead of O(nk). The same idea is used for overlapping text chunks in RAG.

items.name: Recursion & backtracking

resource.label: CampusX · Python for AI · Recursion & Memoization · 45 min

items.note: Recursion is covered here. Backtracking (the "also" link) is recursion that builds a candidate step by step and undoes the last step when it can't lead to a solution: permutations, subsets, sudoku. Pattern: choose → recurse → un-choose.

items.name: BFS & DFS

resource.label: cp-algorithms · Breadth-first search

items.note: No CampusX video covers this. BFS uses a queue and visits level by level, giving shortest paths in unweighted graphs. DFS (the "also" link) uses recursion or a stack and goes deep first: cycle detection, topological order. Both are O(V + E). Always keep a visited set.

items.name: Dynamic programming basics

resource.label: CampusX · Python for AI · Recursion & Memoization @ 19:32–45:06 Memoization — The rabbit problem · 26 min

items.note: DP = recursion + remembering answers to overlapping subproblems. Fibonacci goes from O(2ⁿ) to O(n) with memoisation (functools.lru_cache). Bottom-up means filling a table from the smallest case up.

items.name: Greedy basics

resource.label: Wikipedia · Greedy algorithm

items.note: Greedy takes the locally best choice at each step and never looks back. It's fast, and correct only for some problems (activity selection, Huffman coding, coin change with standard coins). LLM greedy decoding is exactly this: pick the top token each step.

items.name: Complexity of vector similarity search

resource.label: Pinecone · Vector indexes (Faiss series)

items.note: Brute-force search compares the query with all n vectors of dimension d: O(n·d) per query. 1M × 768 dims is about 768M multiply-adds. Approximate indexes (IVF, HNSW in the "also" link) get roughly O(log n) by accepting a small recall loss.

items.name: Batching & chunking efficiency

resource.label: Batching & chunking efficiency

items.note: Batching amortises fixed per-call costs (network round-trip, GPU kernel launch): embedding 1,000 texts in batches of 100 is 10 calls instead of 1,000. Chunking bounds memory and context: split long documents into overlapping windows. Trade-off: bigger batches mean more throughput but higher latency and memory per call.

items.name: Caching strategies

resource.label: Wikipedia · Cache replacement policies

items.note: A cache stores results so repeated work is O(1). LRU evicts the least recently used item (functools.lru_cache, the "also" link). In LLM apps: exact-match response caches, embedding caches keyed by a text hash, semantic caches, and provider prompt caching.

items.name: Graph traversal for agent planning

resource.label: Anthropic · Building effective agents — Orchestrator-workers

items.note: Agent workflows are directed graphs: nodes are steps (LLM calls, tools), edges are transitions, possibly conditional. Running one is a traversal, and planning is search over it. Keep a visited set or a step limit so loops end (LangGraph's recursion limit is exactly this).

items.note: Map-reduce summarisation: split the document into chunks, summarise each chunk independently (map, which can run in parallel), then combine the chunk summaries into one final summary (reduce). items.name: Behavior Adaptation vs Knowledge Injection

resource.label: Karpathy · Intro to LLMs @ 14:14–17:52 Finetuning into an Assistant · 4 min

items.note: Behaviour adaptation (style, format, task skill) is what fine-tuning does well. Knowledge injection (new facts) is better done with RAG, which is updatable, citable and doesn't require retraining.

items.name: Prompt Steering vs Weight Updates

resource.label: OpenAI docs · Optimizing accuracy — Prompt engineering

items.note: Prompt steering changes the input each time: instant, reversible, costs tokens on every call. A weight update (fine-tuning) changes the model itself: persistent, cheaper per call, but slow to iterate and harder to undo. Steer first, and update weights only for stable, high-volume behaviour.

items.name: Latency & Cost Considerations

resource.label: Fine-tuning vs RAG vs prompting — latency & cost

items.note: Latency and cost: long prompts and RAG context add input tokens and latency to every call. A fine-tuned smaller model can match a big prompted model on a narrow task at a fraction of the cost and latency, but it adds training and hosting costs. Compare on your own traffic volume.

items.name: Maintenance Overhead

resource.label: Fine-tuning vs RAG vs prompting — maintenance

items.note: Maintenance: prompts are edited in minutes. RAG needs index upkeep (re-ingesting, freshness). Fine-tuned models need retraining when data or the base model changes, plus eval reruns and adapter versioning. Pick the lightest option that meets the quality bar.

items.name: Task-Specific Metrics

resource.label: CampusX · How to Evaluate LLM Applications @ 4:29–5:50 Define Success Criteria and Metrics · 1 min

items.note: Task-specific metrics: pick metrics that match the task, like exact match or F1 for extraction, accuracy for classification, pass@k for code, and a rubric-based LLM judge for open-ended writing. Measure them on a held-out set.

items.name: Format Accuracy

resource.label: CampusX · How to Evaluate LLM Applications @ 4:29–5:50 Define Success Criteria and Metrics · 1 min

items.note: Format accuracy = the share of outputs that follow the required format (valid JSON, correct fields, allowed values). Check it with a parser or validator on every eval run.

items.name: Behavioral Consistency

resource.label: Anthropic Docs · Increase output consistency

items.note: Behavioural consistency: the model gives the same kind of answer for similar inputs and across repeated runs. Measure the variance across reruns and paraphrases, and use low temperature, examples and structured outputs to reduce it.

items.name: Fast production deployment

resource.label: When to use managed platforms — fast deployment

items.note: Use a managed platform when you need to ship fast: models are one API call away, and scaling, auth, logging and billing are already solved, so the team builds the product instead of infrastructure.

items.name: Enterprise compliance needs

resource.label: AWS Bedrock docs · Compliance validation

items.note: Enterprise needs (data residency, private networking, audit logs, certifications, one vendor contract) are the strongest reason to use Claude or other models through the company's existing cloud.

items.name: Reduced infra management

resource.label: When to use managed platforms — reduced infra

items.note: Reduced infra management: no GPU procurement, driver updates, model serving stack, autoscaling or failover to run. The trade-off is less control over each of those.

items.name: Multi-model experimentation

resource.label: AWS Bedrock docs · What is Amazon Bedrock

items.note: Managed platforms offer many models (Claude, Llama, Mistral, etc.) behind one API and one bill, which makes it easy to A/B test models on the same eval set.

items.name: Vendor lock-in

resource.label: Managed platforms trade-off — vendor lock-in

items.note: Vendor lock-in: platform-specific APIs, IAM, guardrails and knowledge-base features make switching expensive. Reduce it with a thin model-client interface in your code, prompts and evals kept in your repo, and portable data stores.

items.name: Limited model customization

resource.label: Managed platforms trade-off — limited customisation

items.note: Limited customisation: you can usually only fine-tune the models and methods the platform offers, can't change the serving stack (quantisation, decoding tricks, custom kernels), and new model versions or features may arrive later than on the provider's own API.

items.name: Cost considerations

resource.label: Managed platforms trade-off — cost

items.note: Cost: pay-per-token is cheap at low volume, but at high steady volume, reserved throughput or self-hosting an open model can be cheaper. Include hidden costs (logging, data transfer, guardrail calls) and compare against your real traffic.

items.name: Less low-level control

resource.label: Managed platforms trade-off — less control

items.note: Less low-level control: no access to weights, logits or the batching and scheduling setup, limited visibility into why latency spikes, and you rely on the provider's roadmap and uptime. Self-hosting gives full control at the cost of running it yourself.
